stages.title: Language sounds and pronunciation
stages.hook: Say "khalav" (milk) and "lekhem" (bread). Can you feel the rough "kh" sound in your throat?
explain: Hebrew has five clear vowel sounds: a, e, i, o, u. They are short and do not change. The letter ח (khet) makes a rough "kh" sound, like the end of the Scottish word "loch". The letter ר (resh) is said at the back of the mouth by most speakers today.
In Hebrew most words are stressed on the last part: khalav, sefer. Some words are stressed on the next-to-last part, and in this course we mark that with an accent, as in shémesh (sun).
This course uses Modern Hebrew, the everyday language of Israel. The words are shown with small vowel marks called niqqud, so you can read them aloud.
stages.mnemonic: Khalav and lekhem: rough "kh" for milk and bread.
sentences: The moon is in the sky.

gq.q: Which Hebrew letter makes a rough "kh" sound?
gq.why: Khet makes the rough sound in khalav (milk).

gq.q: How many vowel sounds does Hebrew have?
gq.why: Hebrew has five vowel sounds: a, e, i, o, u.

panel.q: Why does the word "yaréakh" have an accent mark in this course?
o: It shows the stress is not on the last part of the word
It shows the word is plural, which is rare in Hebrew
It shows the word is a question
panel.why: Most Hebrew words are stressed at the end, so unusual stress is marked.

panel.q: What do niqqud marks show?
panel.why: Niqqud are small points and dashes that show vowels.

panel.q: Name one Hebrew sound that does not exist in standard English and give a word with it.
panel.model: The rough kh in khalav (milk) or lekhem (bread) is not in standard English.
panel.why: The rough kh sound comes from the back of the mouth.

teach.model: Hebrew has five clear vowels. The letter khet makes a rough kh sound, as in khalav for milk. Most words are stressed on the last part.

points.ask: Where is the loud part of a word?

stages.title: Alphabet, script or basic characters
stages.hook: Hebrew goes from right to left. Where on a page do you think the first letter sits?
explain: Hebrew is written from right to left. The alphabet, called the alef-bet, has 22 letters. There are no capital letters. In printed Hebrew the letters are separate and do not join, unlike Arabic.

Five letters change shape at the end of a word: ך ם ן ף ץ. Some letters look alike, such as ב and כ or ד and ר, so look carefully. A dot inside some letters, called a dagesh, can change the sound: בּ is "b" but ב is "v".
Letter names: alef, bet, gimel, dalet, hey, vav, zayin, khet. Adults usually write without niqqud, but books for children and learners add them.
stages.mnemonic: Alef, bet, gimel, dalet: like the first four stairs of a staircase going left.
sentences: Hebrew is written from right to left.

gq.q: How many letters are in the Hebrew alphabet?

gq.why: Hebrew runs from right to left.

panel.q: The letter בּ (with a dot) is "b" and ב (no dot) is "v". What is the dot called?
panel.why: The dagesh dot changes the sound of some letters.

panel.q: Why does the letter מ look different at the end of a word (ם)?
o: Five letters have a special final form
It is a spelling mistake that printers keep making
panel.why: Final forms are a feature of five letters: ך ם ן ף ץ.

panel.q: How is the Hebrew script different from Arabic?
o: Hebrew letters stay separate and do not join
Hebrew letters always join, just like in Arabic script
panel.why: Printed Hebrew letters do not join to one another.

teach.model: Hebrew has 22 letters and is written from right to left. Letters do not join. Five letters have a final form. A dot called dagesh can change the sound.

stages.title: Greetings and introductions
stages.hook: The word "shalom" means hello, goodbye and peace. Why would one word do all three jobs?
explain: Shalom means "peace" and is used for both hello and goodbye. In the morning say boker tov, "good morning", and in the evening erev tov. At night say layla tov. On Friday and Saturday people say Shabbat shalom, "a peaceful Sabbath".
To ask "how are you?" a man hears ma shlomkha and a woman hears ma shlomekh. In Hebrew the "you" form changes for a man and a woman. Replies: tov, toda (good, thanks).
Toda means "thank you", and bevakasha means both "please" and "you are welcome". Hebrew is a language where one short word can carry many polite jobs.
stages.mnemonic: Shalom: peace at the start, peace at the end.
sentences: I am from the city of Haifa.

gq.why: Shalom is peace and is used to greet and to leave.

gq.q: How do you ask a woman "how are you?"

panel.q: Why do a man and a woman hear different forms of "how are you?"
o: Hebrew "you" changes with the age of the person
panel.why: Hebrew marks the gender of the person you speak to.

panel.q: What does "bevakasha" mean?
o: Both please and you are welcome
Only thank you, said when receiving a gift
panel.why: Bevakasha is used when asking and when answering thanks.

panel.q: What is said on Friday evening and Saturday?
o: Layla tov, said when going to bed
panel.why: Shabbat shalom wishes a peaceful Sabbath.

teach.model: Say shalom to greet and to leave. Say boker tov in the morning and erev tov in the evening. Say toda for thank you and bevakasha for please.

points.ask: How do I say good morning?
How do I say thank you and please?

stages.title: Numbers and counting
stages.hook: In Hebrew, "three books" and "three cats" use different words for "three". Why might numbers care about gender?
explain: Hebrew has two sets of numbers. Counting alone uses the feminine forms: akhat, shtayim, shalosh, arba, khamesh, shesh, sheva. For masculine nouns use: ekhad, shnayim, shlosha, arba'a, khamisha, shisha, shiv'a, asara.

The number follows a strange rule from 3 to 10: the feminine noun takes the shorter number and the masculine noun takes the longer number with -a. So shlosha sfarim (three books, sefer is masculine) but shalosh milim (three words, mila is feminine).
For ages, say ben (son of) or bat (daughter of): hu ben sheva, "he is seven".
stages.mnemonic: Three to ten look backwards: boys get the long number.

gq.q: "Milim" (words) is feminine. Which is right for "five words"?
gq.why: A feminine noun takes the shorter number: khamesh.

gq.q: Which number do you use when you just count "one, two, three"?
o: The feminine forms: akhat, shtayim, shalosh
The masculine forms: ekhad, shnayim, shlosha

panel.q: A boy says "hu ben shesh". What does he say?
panel.why: Ben + a number gives the age of a boy.

panel.q: Why is it "shlosha yeladim" (three boys) but "shalosh yeladot" (three girls)?
o: Numbers 3–10 take the opposite gender form from the noun
Girls are older, so they get the shorter number
panel.why: Hebrew numbers 3–10 have reverse gender agreement.

panel.q: Which phrase uses the correct number for "ten books"?
panel.why: Sefer is masculine, so the long form asara is used; sfarim is its plural.

teach.model: Hebrew has masculine and feminine numbers. From three to ten the number has the opposite gender of the noun. Counting alone uses feminine forms.

points.ask: What is odd from three to ten?
Which forms do I use to count out loud?

stages.title: Colours and shapes
stages.hook: If a girl and a boy both have a red ball, would the word "red" be the same? Look at the endings!
explain: Colours are adjectives and agree with the noun in gender and number. Masculine singular: adom (red), kakhol (blue), yarok (green), tsahov (yellow), lavan (white), shakhor (black). Feminine adds -a: adumá, kekhulá, yeruká, tsehuvá, levaná, shekhorá.
Adjectives come after the noun: tapuakh adom, a red apple. The plural has -im (masculine) and -ot (feminine): shamayim kekhulim, blue sky.
Shapes: igul (circle), meruba (square), meshulash (triangle). Hebrew has no verb for "to be" in the present: ha-tapuakh adom is "the apple is red".
stages.mnemonic: The colour follows the thing: a girl gets -a.
sentences: The ball is white and black.

gq.q: "Kadur" (ball) is masculine. Which is correct for "a white ball"?
gq.why: A masculine noun takes the masculine adjective, placed after the noun.

panel.q: "Shamayim" (sky) is plural in form. Which adjective ending fits?
panel.why: Shamayim is masculine plural, so the adjective takes -im.

panel.q: Why do we say "tapuakh adom" but "agvaniya aduma"?
o: Tapuakh is masculine and agvaniya (tomato) is feminine
Tomatoes are redder, so the colour word is longer
panel.why: Adjectives agree in gender.

panel.q: What is missing from "ha-tapuakh adom" compared with English "The apple is red"?
o: The word "is", which Hebrew leaves out in the present
The word "the" before the noun, which Hebrew skips
panel.why: Hebrew has no separate present-tense "is" in such sentences.

teach.model: Colours are adjectives. They come after the noun and match its gender and number. Hebrew has no word for is here.

points.ask: What kind of word is a colour?

stages.title: Family and people
stages.hook: In Hebrew you can call your mum "ima". Say it slowly: what two sounds start and end the word?
explain: Family words: ima (mum), abba (dad), akh (brother), akhot (sister), saba (grandpa), savta (grandma), yeled (boy), yalda (girl). The family is mishpakha.
To say "my" you can add shelli: ima shelli, my mum. Shelli means "of me". Another way is to attach an ending: akhi (my brother), akhoti (my sister). The shorter forms are common in books and songs.
Hebrew words have gender, and plurals end in -im or -ot: yeladim (children, boys or a mixed group), yeladot (girls). A mixed group uses the masculine plural.
stages.mnemonic: Ima and abba: the first words children say.

gq.why: Shelli is the word for "my" placed after the noun.
A mixed group uses the masculine plural yeladim.

panel.q: How do you say "my brother" in the short form?
panel.why: The ending -i means "my": akhi is my brother and akhoti is my sister.

panel.q: A group has two girls and one boy. Which plural is used?
o: Feminine: yeladot, as there are two girls
panel.why: A mixed group takes the masculine plural.

panel.q: Why is "akhot" (sister) not made from "akh" by adding -a?
o: Some words are irregular: sister has its own form
All words are regular, so akhot is a mistake
panel.why: Hebrew has some irregular family words.

teach.model: Ima is mum and abba is dad. Akh is brother and akhot is sister. Say shelli for my. Plurals end in -im or -ot.

stages.title: Common objects
stages.hook: Point at the door and say "delet". Now say "the door". What small piece do you add at the start?
explain: Objects: shulkhan (table), kise (chair), delet (door), khalon (window), et (pen), tik (bag), maftéakh (key), kadur (ball). Hebrew puts "ha-" in front of a noun to say "the": ha-delet, the door.
Many nouns ending in -a or -t are feminine, such as delet (door) and mita (bed). There are exceptions: laila (night) is masculine. Learn the gender with each new noun.
Small words show place: al (on), be- (in), takhat (under). Be- attaches to the noun: ba-tik, in the bag.
stages.mnemonic: Ha- in front means "the": ha-delet, ha-et.
sentences: The pen is on the table.
The key is in the bag.

gq.q: What does "ha-" at the start of a word mean?

gq.why: Al means on; be- is in; takhat is under.

panel.q: What does "ba-tik" mean?
panel.why: Be- + ha- becomes ba-: in the bag.

panel.q: Why must we learn the gender of each noun?
o: Adjectives and verbs must agree with it
Gender is only for people, not for objects such as a door
panel.why: Agreement depends on the noun's gender.

panel.q: How do you say "the key is under the table"?
panel.why: Takhat means under.

teach.model: Hebrew uses ha- for the. The words al, be and takhat mean on, in and under. Learn the gender with each noun.

points.ask: How do I say where something is?
Why do I learn the gender?

stages.title: Everyday actions
stages.hook: Mime reading, writing and running. In Hebrew the verb for a boy and a girl is not the same. Can you spot the clue?
explain: Hebrew verbs have a root of usually three letters. The root כ־ת־ב (k-t-v) is about writing: kotev (writes), ktav (handwriting), mikhtav (letter), katvan (a writer). The root stays and the pattern around it makes new words.
In the present tense the verb shows gender and number, not person. A man says ani kotev (I write), a woman says ani kotevet. Plural: kotvim (m.), kotvot (f.).
Common verbs, present masculine singular: okhel (eats), shote (drinks), holekh (walks), yashen (sleeps), kore (reads), kotev (writes), mesakhek (plays), ratz (runs).
stages.mnemonic: The root is a tree trunk: k-t-v grows kotev, ktav, mikhtav.
sentences: The boy plays in the garden.

gq.q: A woman says "I write". Which is correct?
gq.why: In the present tense, the verb has a feminine form ending in -et.

gq.q: Which letters make the root of kotev, ktav and mikhtav?
gq.why: The shared letters k-t-v carry the idea of writing.

panel.q: Why does the present tense not show "I", "you" and "he"?
o: It shows gender and number; the pronoun is a separate word
It never shows anything, so context decides gender
panel.why: Present forms are participles, which agree in gender and number.

panel.q: What is the feminine of "shote" (drinks)?
panel.why: Feminine singular ends in -a for this verb.

panel.q: Which word probably relates to writing?
o: shulkhan (table), because it has a kh sound
panel.why: It has the root k-t-v.

teach.model: Most Hebrew words grow from a three-letter root. The present tense changes with gender and number. A man says kotev and a woman says kotevet.

points.ask: How does the present verb change?

stages.title: Simple listening and speaking
stages.hook: You are in a talk and do not understand. Which little phrases keep the conversation going?
explain: Useful words: ken (yes), lo (no), bevakasha (please), slikha (sorry or excuse me), ani mevin (I understand, a man), ani lo mevin (I do not understand), tagid shuv (say it again, to a man), le'at (slowly), ma ze? (what is this?).
The word slikha is very common: it works for "excuse me" in a crowd and for "sorry". A woman says ani mevina, with -a at the end. When talking to a woman, "say it again" is tagidi shuv.
Listening tip: Hebrew stress is usually on the last part. Repeat after a speaker, copy the rhythm and say the throat sound kh clearly.
stages.mnemonic: Slikha: one word for sorry and excuse me.
sentences: I do not understand the word.

gq.q: A woman wants to say "I understand". Which form?

o: Thank you, said after a favour

panel.q: Why does the woman form of "tagid shuv" end in -i (tagidi)?
o: Commands change with the gender of the listener
It is a plural, so the ending is -i as in yeladim
panel.why: Hebrew commands have different forms for men and women.

panel.q: Where is the stress in most Hebrew words?
panel.why: Final stress is the norm.

panel.q: Which phrase asks someone to talk more slowly?
o: ken, toda, meaning yes and thanks
panel.why: Le'at means slowly.

teach.model: Say ken for yes and lo for no. Say slikha for sorry or excuse me. If you do not understand, say ani lo mevin, and ask someone to say it again with tagid shuv.

points.ask: How do I say yes and no?
How do I say I do not understand?
